Assyria
ăs-sĭr'ĭ-ă
n. (the Mesopotamian empire on the upper Tigris — the rod of God's anger against Israel, and the rod He afterward broke)
From Hebrew 'Ashshur, Asshur — at once the second son of Shem (Gen 10:22), the national god, the capital city, and the land. The Greek Assyria comes through the same name.

Biblical Definition

Assyria is the first world empire Scripture sets over against the covenant people, and Isaiah gives the doctrine of it in one line: “O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation” (Isa 10:5). The empire that deported the ten tribes was a tool in the hand of God — not a rival power He was forced to tolerate, but an instrument He raised, aimed, and afterward burned, “for he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it” (Isa 10:13), and the axe that boasts against the hand that swings it is broken for its boasting. The great fact of Assyrian history in the Bible is 2Ki 17:6: Samaria taken, Israel carried away, settled in Halah and Habor and the cities of the Medes, and never restored as a kingdom. Judah, spared by a single night's judgment on Sennacherib's camp — “the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand” (Isa 37:36) — learned nothing from it, and went to Babylon a century later. Yet Assyria is not left under sentence only. Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and Isaiah sees a day when the LORD will say, “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance” (Isa 19:25) — the empire of the rod brought in among the worshippers.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives Assyria as an ancient kingdom of Asia, on the Tigris, whose capital was Nineveh, and derives the name from Asshur, son of Shem.

expand to see more

ASSYRIA, n. An ancient kingdom of Asia, lying east of the Tigris, named from Asshur, the son of Shem.

Its capital was Nineveh, a city of exceeding greatness, built by Nimrod or Asshur.

Under Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser and Sennacherib it subdued Syria, Samaria and the coast, and threatened Jerusalem.

The ten tribes were carried thence into captivity in the ninth year of Hoshea.

The empire fell to the Chaldeans and Medes, and Nineveh was destroyed, as Nahum and Zephaniah foretold.

Key Scripture

Isa 10:5 — "O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation."

2Ki 17:6 — "In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes."

Isa 37:36 — "Then the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses."

Isa 19:25 — "Whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance."

Modern Corruption

Empires are read as autonomous political forces and Israel's fall as ordinary geopolitics; Isa 10 says the empire was a rod God held, which makes the whole account one of covenant judgment, not power politics.

expand to see more

The standard modern account of the fall of Samaria is a study in Iron Age power: Assyrian siege technology, deportation policy, tribute economics. Every fact of it may be granted, and Isaiah still contradicts the account, because Isaiah names the agent. Assyria is a rod, and a rod does not decide where it falls. This is the doctrine of providence applied to the hardest case — God ordains the wicked act of a wicked empire, is not the author of its wickedness, and holds it fully accountable for what He ordained it to do. Isa 10:12 puts both halves side by side: God will punish “the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria” after He has performed His whole work through him. To lose either half is to lose the passage.

The second corruption runs the other way, among Christians: treating Assyria as a monster with no possible mercy. Jonah went to Nineveh precisely because mercy was on offer, and resented it. Isa 19:25 goes further than Jonah could have borne — Egypt called “my people” and Assyria “the work of my hands”, terms elsewhere reserved for Israel. The gospel later broke open on that promise. The nation God uses as a rod today is a nation to whom He may yet send preachers, and the church that cannot pray for its persecutors has not read the twelve prophets.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Ashshur (H804), Asshur, Assyria; shebet (H7626), a rod; galah (H1540), to carry into exile.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Ashshur (H804) — Asshur; the son of Shem, the god, the city, and the empire, all one name.

Hebrew shebet (H7626) — a rod, a tribe, a sceptre; the instrument Assyria is called in Isa 10:5.

Hebrew matteh (H4294) — a staff; the parallel term in the same verse, the same point twice.

Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, to carry away captive; the verb of the deportation of the ten tribes.

Hebrew ma'aseh yaday — “the work of my hands”; the astonishing title given Assyria in Isa 19:25.

Usage

"“O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger” — the empire named as an instrument."

"“Carried Israel away into Assyria” — the end of the northern kingdom."

"“Assyria the work of my hands” — the rod brought in among the worshippers."
